title: A Orbit for the Protocol Revisited
premise: Marguerite Ravensworth, a xenolinguist whose mind was rewired by contact with the silent Vessh, ferries supplies between dying colony worlds while hiding the fact that he no longer dreams in any human tongue. When the children of Meridian Colony begin sharing one dream—a signal the Vessh buried in the cryosleep archive that holds half of humanity's frozen sleepers—Marguerite is the only person who can translate it. The message is a choice: the Vessh will preserve either the waking colonists or the sleepers, but not both, and their patience expires in weeks. Marguerite, who belongs fully to neither species, teaches the children to answer in a language made of both, forcing the Vessh to accept a third option—coexistence—and finally giving him a family that speaks every part of who he is.
about_author: Astrid Iversen is a former maritime radio operator who spent a decade listening to languages she never learned to speak. She writes from a converted lighthouse on the Norwegian coast, where she insists the fog signals count as dialogue.

chapters.title: The Long Route
chapters.summary: Marguerite pilots the freighter Long Silence between abandoned relay stations, cataloguing worlds that have gone quiet. In POV close-third, we learn he hasn't dreamed in English for six years and records his Vessh-shaped dreams in a private log. Emotional beat: loneliness worn as routine.

chapters.title: Meridian, Still Awake
chapters.summary: Arriving at Meridian Colony, Marguerite trades translation services for fuel. The colony administrator, Dara Okonkwo, treats him with wary kindness; her daughter Sefu asks him what the stars say back. He lies fluently. Beat: the ache of being almost-home but never home.

chapters.title: Children of the Same Night
chapters.summary: Sefu and eleven other children report identical dreams: a corridor of sleeping faces and a voice counting down. Dara summons Marguerite privately—he's the only xenolinguist within forty light-years. Beat: dread arriving disguised as duty.

chapters.title: What the Dream Says
chapters.summary: Marguerite interviews the children, recognizing Vessh grammatical structures in their drawings. The dream is a message, and it names the cryosleep vault beneath Meridian where 40,000 sleepers wait. Beat: his hidden fluency becomes a debt coming due.

chapters.title: The Vault Below
chapters.summary: Descended into the cryosleep archive, Marguerite finds Vessh script grown into the coolant conduits like frost. The sleepers' stasis fields are being read, weighed. His POV reveals he once bargained with the Vessh to save his own mind—at a price he's never confessed. Beat: guilt surfacing.

chapters.title: Dara's Question
chapters.summary: Dara confronts Marguerite about what he isn't telling her; the children's dreams are accelerating, some now refusing to wake. He admits the message is real but hides the choice it contains. Beat: intimacy built on partial truth begins to crack.

chapters.title: Counting Down
chapters.summary: The children synchronize: they all dream the same night, same hour. Marguerite deciphers the deadline—nineteen days. The Vessh vessel appears at the system's edge, vast and patient. Beat: the clock starts, and denial ends.

chapters.title: Two Halves of One Ship
chapters.summary: Colony council demands answers; panic spreads when the vault's power draw spikes. Marguerite proposes contacting the Vessh directly through the children's shared channel. Dara backs him against the council's fear. Beat: found-family loyalty tested by public stakes.

chapters.title: First Contact, Again
chapters.summary: Through a dreaming child as conduit, Marguerite speaks Vessh aloud for the first time in years—the language fits his mouth like an old scar. The Vessh respond: they recognize him, and they are not glad. Beat: reunion as reckoning.

chapters.title: The Bargain Remembered
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: young Marguerite's first contact aboard the survey ship Kestrel, how the Vessh saved his drowning mind by rewriting it, and why he fled. Present-day Dara reads his confession log. Beat: shame transformed into explanation.

chapters.title: The Terms
chapters.summary: The Vessh state their terms plainly: humanity's presence destabilizes their breeding darks. One population may remain—the waking or the sleepers. The children, hearing this through the dream, begin asking which half they belong to. Beat: impossible arithmetic made intimate.

chapters.title: Council of the Waking
chapters.summary: The colony votes on whether to sacrifice the sleepers—strangers, ancestors—to save themselves. Marguerite refuses to translate the vote into Vessh, arguing the question itself is wrong. He's confined. Beat: moral isolation at the center of the crowd.

chapters.title: Sefu's Doorway
chapters.summary: Sefu sneaks into Marguerite's quarters; she dreams more clearly than the others and has seen the Vessh nursery-worlds. She proposes the children answer in a hybrid language—half human, half Vessh—that offers something new. Beat: hope from the smallest voice.

chapters.title: Grammar of Belonging
chapters.summary: Marguerite and the children build the hybrid tongue over feverish days: human metaphor grafted onto Vessh resonance. Each child contributes words from their own lost homes. Beat: creation as communion; the found family forms around language itself.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: A frightened faction raids the vault to sever the Vessh growths, triggering stasis failures. Forty sleepers die before the systems stabilize. The Vessh interpret it as humanity's answer. Beat: catastrophe born of fear, the point of no return.

chapters.title: Silence Descending
chapters.summary: The Vessh vessel moves into orbit; the countdown compresses to three days. Marguerite, released, sees the colony fracturing—some want to fight, some to flee, none can do either. Beat: despair before the last attempt.

chapters.title: The Third Answer
chapters.summary: Marguerite chooses to broadcast the children's hybrid language directly from the vault, using the sleepers' own stasis harmonics as its bass note—the dead and dreaming speaking together. Beat: audacity as love.

chapters.title: Audience with the Dark
chapters.summary: Climax: Marguerite walks out onto the vault's exposed surface to meet the Vessh envoy, translating in real time between two species and himself. He offers coexistence: humans as translators and caretakers of the dark places. The envoy hesitates. Beat: everything wagered on a single voice.

chapters.title: What the Children Woke To
chapters.summary: The Vessh accept conditionally—the sleepers will wake slowly, integrated, taught the hybrid tongue from birth. The children, exhausted, stop sharing one dream and start sharing one morning. Beat: relief that costs something real.

chapters.title: Waking Numbers
chapters.summary: The first sleepers rise to a changed world and wary hosts. Marguerite mediates the first arguments, small and human and survivable. Dara tells him he could stay. Beat: belonging offered without conditions.

chapters.title: A Language With Windows
chapters.summary: Months later, Marguerite teaches the first joint class of waking adults and children, the hybrid language finding its rhythm. He still dreams in Vessh—but now he translates his dreams aloud at breakfast, and people listen. Beat: integration, quiet and earned.

chapters.title: The Route Home
chapters.summary: Epilogue: Marguerite takes the Long Silence out on one last supply run—not fleeing, but ferrying, carrying letters between worlds that speak again. Sefu rides along as apprentice. He logs the dream of the night before in both languages. Beat: departure that is no longer escape.
